title: Battery-Powered Ships Sail Past the 2,000-Vessel Milestone
summary: The maritime industry touts a milestone of over 2,000 "battery-powered" vessels, yet this figure demands critical assessment. A significant 68% are hybrid configurations, indicating persistent reliance on fossil fuel engines for propulsion and power generation. Real progress will be measured by verifiable reductions in carbon intensity and avoidance of FuelEU Maritime penalties, not by the sheer number of ships equipped with auxiliary batteries.
content:
The maritime industry’s decarbonization transition has reached another historic milestone, with the global fleet of battery-powered commercial vessels officially surpassing the 2,000-ship mark.

Data collected on the Maritime Battery Forum (MBF) Ship Registry confirms that 2,000+ commercial ships have been delivered with battery installations or are currently on order. Overall, this fleet represents a massive 2.4 GWh of installed maritime battery capacity, the same electricity to power 240k European homes for the entire day in.

“Reaching 2,000+ ships marks a significant moment for marine electrification,” says Syb ten Cate Hoedemaker, Managing Director of the Maritime Battery Forum. “For years, pure electric applications were primarily limited to small ferries operating on short routes. Thanks to advancements in battery pricing and technology, we are passing a crucial tipping point. It now makes clear economic sense to build larger, fully electric ships, and installations scaling up to 100 MWh per vessel are expected to become a reality soon. This milestone proves the technology is ready to scale.”

The data show that 68% of these vessels operate as hybrids, utilizing a battery in combination with another energy source such as a diesel engine or hydrogen fuel cell. Plug-in hybrid vessels represent 13% of the fleet and 18% are purely electric. Over recent years, the average installed capacity has steadily grown to approximately 1.5 MWh per ship.

While passenger vessels account for the largest segment at 570 ships, the register demonstrates that every type of commercial vessel is now available in a battery-powered configuration. The milestone fleet encompasses a highly diverse profile, including 313 offshore vessels, 265 cargo vessels, 219 fishing vessels, and 149 workboats, alongside hundreds of specialized vessels (145), yachts (116), tugs (83), and cruise ships (83), proving that scalable energy storage can adapt to varied operational requirements across the sector.

Led by Norway, Europe operates most of the documented battery-powered fleet. However, the true global total is substantially larger, as the register currently tracks only 267 ships in China despite the country’s actual fleet being significantly greater.

While these technological milestones are highly encouraging, the Maritime Battery Forum recognizes that market momentum alone cannot fully decarbonize global shipping. To bridge this gap, the sector urgently needs the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), a landmark policy up to adoption at the UN’s International Maritime Organization (IMO) this December. The Framework aims at cutting global shipping’s emissions while generating billions for green financial investments.

“The incredible growth of maritime battery installations proves that zero-emission technologies are available today, but market momentum alone isn’t enough,” states Madadh MacLaine, Secretary-General of the Zero Emissions Ship Technology Association (ZESTAs). “Regulatory pressure and ambitious global frameworks are essential to scaling up these technologies even further. Only a strong global fuel standard and pricing mechanism can drive the global uptake of zero-emission fuels and technologies, including batteries.”
